q: You skipper a 22 m motor yacht on an overnight passage. At 0310 the watch reports a crew member missing. How do you turn to search?
a: Williamson turn: hard over, at 60° off hard back to 045°T
o: Anderson turn: hard over and round 250° to the spot
Hard over and hold it right round onto 045°T
Stop both engines and let him drift down to you
why: Time unknown: the Williamson turn puts you back on your own track, reciprocal 225° − 180° = 045°T, to search along it.

fig.title: Crew missing
lines: Last seen in the cockpit at 0245

q: Your man overboard is alongside on a line, exhausted, and cannot help himself. Where and how do you get him aboard?
a: Amidships to leeward, lifted level in the net on a halyard
o: At the bathing platform, where the freeboard is lowest
Up the boarding ladder over the side, by his own effort
Amidships, by two crew pulling him up by the arms
why: In a seaway the stern slams near the props; lift him level amidships to leeward — a vertical lift can make him collapse.

fig.title: Recovery
lines: Sea 2.5 m, the stern rising 2 m
Bathing platform aft, props below it
Recovery net and spare halyard ready

q: At 0140 the engine-room fire alarm sounds on your 24 m motor yacht. Before you pull the fixed system's release, what do you do?
a: Stop engines, generator and fans, shut the flaps, count everyone out
o: Open the engine-room door to judge the size of the fire
Keep the engines running to make the nearest port
Run the extractor fans to clear the smoke for the agent
why: Running engines and fans draw the agent out and feed air in; shut the space tight and make sure nobody is inside.

lines: Camera: flames by the starboard engine

q: Your fixed system discharged into the engine room at 0144. At 0150 the engineer wants to open the door to see if the fire is out. What do you tell him?
a: Keep it shut; wait, cool the bulkhead, extinguisher ready
o: Open it now, so the smoke can clear before it spreads
Open it a crack, just enough to look inside
Open it now and start the engines to vent it
why: Opening early lets air in to hot metal and the fire re-ignites; wait the time on the label and let it cool first.

fig.title: After discharge
lines: Now 0150; bulkhead still hot to the touch
System label: keep closed at least 15 min

q: You are holed 110 M from land and estimate the inflow below. With all three pumps running, where do you stand?
a: Gaining about 4 L/min — only just
o: Gaining about 28 L/min — comfortably
Losing about 8 L/min — slowly
Losing about 55 L/min — fast
why: Electric 3600/60 × 0.6 = 36, engine 120, hand 0.7 × 40 = 28: 184 L/min against 180 in — gaining 4.

fig.title: Damage control
lines: Electric: 3,600 L/h rated, 60 % at this head
Hand pump: 0.7 L a stroke, 40 strokes/min

q: You have hit a submerged object 115 M from land and water is pouring in through the split below. What stops most of it?
a: A collision mat over the outside, held on by lines under the hull
o: A mattress pressed against the tank from inside
Heel her to port with the crew's weight to steady her
Speed up so the bow wave keeps the water out
why: Outside, the sea pressure pushes the mat into the split; from inside it pushes the patch away.

fig.title: Damage forward
lines: Can't be reached inside: a tank in the way
Sailcloth, lines and a mattress aboard

q: After hitting a log, a hull panel by the forward bulkhead has cracked and bulges inward as each wave strikes. How do you hold it?
a: Pad and board over it, shored to the bulkhead with wedges
o: Shore it down to the cabin sole, which is closer
Tape it from inside and keep a watch on it
Leave it alone — bracing would split it further
why: A shore spreads the load through a pad and board to a strong point; wedges tighten it as it settles.

fig.title: Forward cabin
lines: Panel cracked, bulging in with each wave
Timber offcuts, wedges, a hatch board

q: Your 24 m motor yacht has run onto a sand bar at the end of a passage. The hull is dry inside. How do you get her off?
a: Kedge out astern, shift weight aft, haul off near high water
o: Full astern on both engines at once
Full ahead to drive her over the bar
Twist her off with the engines and bow thruster
why: Sand drawn into the raw-water intakes can wreck the engines; a kedge and the rising tide get her off safely.

fig.title: Aground on sand
lines: Tide rising: HW in 2 h, 0.8 m to come

q: You have abandoned to the liferaft 110 M offshore and are clear of the yacht, with the EPIRB transmitting. What do you do in the first hour?
a: Seasick pills for all, inflate the floor, set a lookout rota
o: A drink of water for all to keep up strength
Open the canopy wide for air and a better view
Paddle in turns towards the coast, 110 M off
why: Seasickness dehydrates fast, the floor insulates against the cold, and a lookout must not miss a rescuer.

fig.title: In the raft
lines: Raft pack: water, seasick pills, pump

q: There are six of you in the liferaft. Following the raft's instructions, how long from abandoning will your water last?
a: About 3.5 days
o: About 2.5 days
About 2.25 days
About 15 days
why: Day 1 dry; then 7.5 L ÷ (6 × 0.5 L) = 2.5 days: 3.5 days from abandoning.

fig.title: Water in the raft
lines: Raft pack 3.0 L, grab bag 4.5 L
Instructions: no water for the first 24 h
Then 0.5 L per person per day

q: A helicopter is lifting a casualty from your aft deck and has asked you to hold a course and speed. The helmsman keeps looking up at it. What do you tell him?
a: Steer by the compass and hold course and speed steady
o: Turn towards the helicopter to keep it in sight
Slow down whenever the winchman nears the deck
Follow the helicopter's movements to stay under it
why: The pilot holds station on you; a steady course and speed is what he asked for, and any change upsets the lift.

q: The MRCC will send a helicopter for your injured crew once you are inside its radius of action, and asks you to close its base. When will you be inside it?
a: About 0800, after 6 h at 7.5 kn
o: About 0700, after 5 h at 9 kn
About 0617, after 4 h 17 min at 10.5 kn
About 0000 tomorrow, after 22 h at 7.5 kn
why: 165 − 120 = 45 M to go at 9 − 1.5 = 7.5 kn over the ground: 6 h, so 0800.

fig.title: MRCC
lines: You: 165 M from its base, heading for it

q: A crew member has had severe abdominal pain for six hours and is getting worse. How do you get a doctor's advice from here?
a: MF DSC urgency call to the coast station, then PAN-PAN on MF
o: VHF DSC distress alert, then MAYDAY on channel 16
PAN-PAN on channel 16 to the coast station
Wait for landfall tomorrow and see a doctor ashore
why: Medical advice is urgency, not distress; 100 M off only the MF station hears you, and the MRCC links you to a doctor.

fig.title: 100 M offshore
lines: Coast station: VHF to about 30 M
MF DSC watch on 2187.5 kHz to 150 M
Yacht has VHF DSC and MF/HF DSC

q: At night 90 M offshore the mast goes over the side. It lies to leeward, still held by the rigging, and punches the hull on every wave. What do you do?
a: Cut it free; start the engine only once no line is in the water
o: Start the engine and motor away to pull clear of it
Haul it back aboard over the side to save the rig
Leave it alongside as a sea anchor until daylight
why: In this sea the spar will hole the hull: knock out the pins, cut the wires, and keep the prop still until every line is aboard.

fig.title: Dismasted
lines: Mast and boom in the water to leeward

q: 120 M from land the steering suddenly goes slack. A look over the stern shows the rudder blade has broken off. How do you steer?
a: Tow a drogue on a bridle and steer by its two legs
o: Fit the emergency tiller to the stock and steer
Lash the wheel amidships and sail on as she goes
Steer by moving the crew's weight fore and aft
why: With no blade the stock steers nothing; a drogue on a bridle, one leg shortened, turns her the way you want.

fig.title: Steering failure
lines: Sea 2 m, wind F5 on the quarter
Drogue, warps and spare blocks aboard

q: On your twin-engine motor yacht the hydraulic steering fails, with the rudders jammed amidships. How do you steer to safety?
a: With the engines: more power on one side than the other
o: With the bow thruster alone, at cruising speed
You cannot steer — anchor and wait for a tow
With one engine only, the other one shut down
why: Twin screws steer her: ahead harder on the port engine turns her to starboard, and the other way round.

q: At 0130, 110 M offshore, the alternator belt breaks and there is no spare. The engine still runs. What do you keep switched on?
a: Nav lights and the VHF; plot by DR and fixes on paper
o: The plotter and autopilot, as they navigate for you
Everything until the alarm sounds, then nothing
The fridge and cabin lights; VHF only to call
why: With no charge, save the battery for what keeps you seen and heard — the lights and the radio; a paper plot needs no power.

q: You are 120 M off the coast of a state that publishes this GMDSS coverage. In which sea area are you?
a: A2 — inside MF DSC cover, outside VHF
o: A1 — still within this state's cover
A3 — beyond VHF, so on satellite only
A4 — no shore station keeps watch
why: A1 is VHF DSC coverage; A2 is MF DSC coverage beyond it; A3 and A4 lie beyond both.

fig.title: Coast state GMDSS notice
lines: VHF DSC watch: to about 30 M
MF DSC watch, 2187.5 kHz: to about 150 M

q: You sent an MF DSC distress alert 140 M offshore and the coast station has acknowledged it by DSC. Where do you now make your MAYDAY call?
a: By voice on 2182 kHz
o: By voice on VHF channel 16
By voice on 2187.5 kHz
By voice on VHF channel 70
why: The voice call follows on the frequency paired with the DSC one: 2187.5 kHz DSC → 2182 kHz voice.

q: To save paper on a three-day passage you set the NAVTEX to accept the weather forecasts only. What else will it still print?
a: Nav warnings, gale warnings and SAR alerts
o: Nothing — it prints only the types you pick
Only gale warnings for the sea area you are in
Everything, once you are within 50 M of a station
why: Navigational (A) and meteorological (B) warnings and SAR messages (D) cannot be switched off on a NAVTEX receiver.

q: You bought this yacht last month and leave tomorrow on a 140 M crossing. What do you do about the EPIRB?
a: Register it in your name on the flag state's beacon register
o: Nothing — it sends its position whoever owns it
Re-register it only if you rename the yacht
Switch it on briefly to check it reaches a satellite
why: The MRCC calls the registered contacts first, and a stale entry wastes hours. Test it only with the test button.

fig.title: EPIRB check
lines: Coded for the yacht's flag state

q: In the liferaft at night your SART's indicator changes as its label describes below. What does it tell you?
a: A ship's or aircraft's radar is sweeping you — flares ready
o: The battery is low — switch it off to save it
A satellite has fixed your position for the MRCC
The MRCC has acknowledged your distress alert
why: A radar SART answers X-band radar pulses; the change means a radar is in range, so keep a lookout and use flares.

fig.title: SART label
lines: Standby: lamp flashes every few seconds
Interrogated: fast flashing and a beeper

q: At 0220, 90 M offshore, your VHF DSC sounds a distress alert from a yacht 25 M upwind that you cannot reach in this gale. Five minutes on, nobody has acknowledged it. How do you pass it on?
a: MF DSC relay to the coast station alone, then MAYDAY RELAY to it
o: VHF DSC relay to all ships, so the nearest one hears
Re-send her alert as your own DSC distress alert
Nothing — the coast station must have heard it too
why: Out of VHF range of the shore, relay to the coast station on MF; a DSC relay to all ships only sets off more alarms.

q: A distress has been going on for an hour on channel 16 when you hear the MRCC's broadcast below. What may you now do on 16?
a: Brief, essential calls only — the distress is not over
o: Normal working again — the distress is finished
Nothing at all until the MRCC lifts the silence
Only the vessel in distress may transmit on 16
why: PRUDONCE allows restricted working while the distress goes on; SEELONCE FEENEE would end it.

fig.title: Heard on channel 16
lines: ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS

q: At 0340, 95 M offshore, you pass a container floating awash. What does the law expect of you?
a: SÉCURITÉ to ships near, and report it to the coast station
o: Note it in the log; report it at your next port
A MAYDAY, since it endangers every vessel
Nothing — reporting is for merchant ships
why: SOLAS V/31: every master reports a direct danger to navigation to ships nearby and to the authorities ashore.

fig.title: On watch
lines: Shipping lane 10 M to the north
MF/HF DSC and a sat phone aboard

q: At 0500 you hear this MAYDAY. The owner, aboard as a guest, tells you to carry on: he has people to meet at 1800. What do you do?
a: Go to her with all speed and tell her and the MRCC
o: Carry on — a yacht need only relay the MAYDAY
Go only if the owner agrees — it is his yacht
Stand by on 16 until the MRCC tells you to go
why: SOLAS V/33: a master able to help must go with all speed; if he does not, the reason goes in the log.

fig.title: Channel 16
lines: Your ETA at her: about 2 h

q: At night you collided with a fishing boat; one of your crew is hurt and both vessels are damaged. Once everyone is safe, what do you do about the records?
a: Keep the log, plotter track and AIS data as they are, and report
o: Write a fair copy of the log before you report
Wait for the fishing boat to report — she was give-way
Report only if your insurer asks you to
why: The investigators need the original records; altering them destroys the evidence, and the report is your duty.

q: The owner wants to sail at 0600 on this 130 M passage to keep to his schedule. Who decides, and what is the decision?
a: You do — you wait for the window, whatever the schedule
o: The owner — the yacht and the schedule are his
The crew, by a vote at the morning briefing
The insurer, who must be phoned for consent
why: SOLAS V/34-1: no owner may stop the master taking a decision he judges needed for safety.

q: You are buying a 20 m yacht with a loan; the bank lends against a mortgage on her. On which register do you put her?
a: The full register, so the mortgage can be recorded
o: The small ships register — cheaper and enough abroad
Either — the bank keeps the bill of sale instead
Neither — a mortgage is held at the bank only
why: Under these rules only the full register records title and mortgages, which is what a lender needs.

fig.title: The flag state's rules say
lines: Full register: title and mortgages recorded
Bank: 60 % of price, secured on the yacht

q: You are checking the papers before sailing for a foreign port. What do you sort out before you leave?
a: Bring the original certificate of registry aboard
o: Nothing — a copy of the registry will do
A second insurance certificate for the crew
The surveyor's report from when you bought her
why: Officials abroad ask for the original certificate of registry as proof of nationality; a copy is often refused.

q: You are about to pay for a used 20 m yacht and the seller hands over the papers below. What must you have before you pay?
a: The mortgage discharged, so the title comes to you clear
o: Nothing more — the signed bill of sale is enough
Only the insurance moved over into your name
A new survey, which clears any debt on her
why: A registered mortgage stays on the yacht after a sale; the lender could arrest her from you.

fig.title: At completion
lines: Bill of sale signed by the seller

q: The owner lent his yacht to a friend with a coastal certificate, who was dismasted 90 M out on a crossing. Is the claim covered?
a: No — the skipper warranty was broken on that passage
o: Yes — the dismasting had nothing to do with her skill
Yes — warranties only matter for third-party claims
Only half — the owner shares the blame with her
why: The policy says a breach suspends cover while it lasts; the loss fell inside the breach, whatever caused it.

fig.title: Policy extract
lines: Warranty: skipper on passages over 60 M
to hold Yachtmaster Offshore or equal
A breach suspends cover while it lasts

q: You plan to take the yacht on this passage on 5 November. Are you covered?
a: No — get the insurer to extend the season first
o: Yes — inside 100 M is all the policy asks
Yes — the season matters only for laying up
Only for third-party claims, not the hull
why: Outside the navigation limits, in area or in time, the yacht is not covered; get a written extension before sailing.

fig.title: Policy limits
lines: Mediterranean, within 100 M of the mainland
Planned route: at most 60 M off

q: At night your 20 m yacht drags her anchor and hits a moored yacht. Both are damaged. What does your insurer pay?
a: The other yacht's damage, not your own
o: Both yachts' damage — it was an accident
Your damage only — she has her own policy
Nothing — a dragging anchor is negligence
why: Third-party cover pays your liability to others; damage to your own yacht needs hull cover.

q: You are filling in the proposal form to insure your new yacht. How do you answer this question?
a: Declare it — a hidden material fact can void the policy
o: Leave it out — it was a different yacht
Leave it out — the claim is paid and closed
Declare it only if the insurer asks again
why: Insurance rests on full disclosure; a past claim is material, and hiding it lets the insurer refuse to pay.

fig.title: Proposal form
lines: 'Any losses or claims in the last 5 years?'
Your old yacht grounded 3 years ago

q: The owner's friends offer to pay him €1,500 each for a week's cruise on his yacht, with you as skipper. What does this do to his insurance?
a: No cover for the trip — paying guests are commercial use
o: Nothing — they are his friends, not customers
Nothing, as long as you hold Offshore
Only the third-party cover is lost; hull stays
why: A private-pleasure policy excludes hire; paying guests make it a charter, and a claim during it would be refused.

q: A charter company offers you a paid job skippering guests on its 18 m yacht for the season. You hold the Yachtmaster Offshore. Can you take it on that certificate?
a: No — the certificate is for recreational use only
o: Yes — Offshore covers any yacht up to 24 m
Yes, if every trip stays within 150 M of land
Yes, if the guests sign a waiver before sailing
why: The Yachtmaster is a recreational certificate; paid skippering needs the flag state's commercial qualification.

fig.title: The flag state's rules say
lines: Skippers paid to carry guests need

q: You leave tomorrow for a foreign port with the crew below. What papers do you prepare for the crew?
a: A crew list with passports, and the deckhand's agreement
o: Only your own passport and certificate
A crew list only — agreements are for merchant ships
The crew's sailing certificates and phone numbers
why: Arrival clearance goes by a crew list and passports; under these rules the paid hand also needs a signed agreement.

fig.title: Departure tomorrow
lines: Flag state's rules: paid crew sign

q: You are arriving from outside the customs area after a 140 M crossing. What do you do about the Q flag and going ashore?
a: Fly Q on arrival; only the skipper goes ashore to report
o: Fly Q only if somebody aboard is ill
Fly Q as you leave your port of departure
All may go ashore; take Q down at the berth
why: Q asks for free pratique: it flies from arrival until you are cleared, and only the skipper lands to report.

fig.title: Pilot book: arrival
lines: Arriving from outside the customs area:
Customs office on the fuel quay

q: You live in the EU and are buying this yacht to keep in the EU. Under the rules below, what must happen?
a: Import her and pay the VAT: temporary admission ends with you
o: Nothing — admission runs on until the 18 months end
Sail out of the EU for a day to start a new 18 months
Re-flag her in the EU, which settles the VAT
why: Temporary admission needs a non-EU owner; an EU resident must import her and pay VAT to keep her in the EU.

fig.title: The customs rules say
lines: a non-EU owner, non-EU flag, up to 18 months
Yacht: non-EU flag, VAT never paid
Buyer: you, resident in the EU

q: A non-EU crew member rejoins you on 1 July for the rest of the season inside the Schengen area. Until what date may she stay?
a: 28 Sep — the Jan–Mar days drop out as she goes
o: 15 Jul — 90 − 75 leaves her only 15 days
8 Jul — 180 days from her first entry
29 Sep — 90 days after the day she arrives
why: As the 180-day window moves on, old days leave it: her count peaks at 83, so she gets 90 days, 1 Jul–28 Sep.

fig.title: Visa rule for her (given)
lines: Entry and exit days both count

q: You signed Lloyd's Open Form with a tug for your disabled yacht. The tow parts in the storm, and she drives ashore and is lost. What is the salvor owed?
a: Nothing — no useful result, no salvage reward
o: His costs for the nine hours he towed
The fixed fee written into the form
A share of the yacht's insured value
why: Under 'no cure, no pay' a reward needs a useful result; the yacht was lost, so nothing is owed.

q: Your engine has failed and the mainsail is torn, but you are in no danger. A commercial tug offers help on channel 16. What do you agree?
a: A towage contract at a price agreed before the line comes over
o: Sign LOF — it costs nothing unless he saves you
Take his line now and settle the bill ashore
Refuse, and ask the coastguard for a lifeboat
why: With no danger, agree a towage price first; taking a line with nothing agreed invites a salvage claim on her value.

fig.title: No danger
lines: Port 50 M off; drifting slowly seaward
Tug offers a tow on channel 16

q: At night your yacht is dragging towards rocks with the engine dead, and a salvage tug offers LOF. The owner is ashore and cannot be reached. Can you sign?
a: Yes — the master may sign a salvage contract for the owner
o: No — only the owner can bind the yacht to a contract
Only once the insurer has agreed by phone
Only with the coastguard as a witness on 16
why: The 1989 Salvage Convention gives the master authority to make salvage contracts on the owner's behalf.

q: After a fuel-filter change there is diesel in the engine bilge with a sheen on it. What do you do with it?
a: Pads and a container; dispose of it ashore
o: Pump it out once you are 12 M offshore
Add detergent so no sheen shows, then pump
Pump it out slowly while under way
why: MARPOL Annex I bans oily discharges; a yacht keeps oily bilge water for shore disposal. Detergent only hides it.

q: At 1500 your holding tank is full. Under the rules below, when may you empty it?
a: At 1800, more than 12 M off and under way
o: Now — 9 M off is well clear of the coast
Now, if you pump it out slowly enough
Never — a holding tank empties only ashore
why: Both conditions must hold — beyond 12 M from land and under way at 4 kn or more — and only at 1800 do they.

fig.title: The flag's sewage rules
lines: Untreated, from the tank: over 12 M off,
under way at 4 kn or more, moderate rate
1500: at anchor, 9 M off the coast
1800: under way, 30 M off at 8 kn

q: You are 60 M offshore in the Mediterranean, under way, with these bags of rubbish. What may go over the side?
a: The food waste only; keep the rest for shore
o: Food waste and cardboard, as both will rot
Glass and tins too, since they sink
Nothing at all — the Med takes no waste
why: MARPOL Annex V: in a special area like the Med only food waste may go, 12 M or more from land and under way.

q: Reading back the night's log, you find that the 0300 entry gives the wrong course. How do you correct it?
a: One line through it, the right course beside, initialled
o: Tear out the page and copy it out again fairly
Correction fluid over it and the right course on top
Rewrite the night's entries neatly in the morning
why: The log is evidence in a claim or an inquiry; a correction must leave the original readable and show who made it.

q: You enter a foreign harbour whose pilot book lists these by-laws. Which rules apply to you inside the port limits?
a: The port's by-laws as well as the COLREGs
o: Only the COLREGs — by-laws bind merchant ships
Only your flag state's rules, as a foreign yacht
Only the by-laws — the COLREGs stop outside
why: Local rules apply alongside the COLREGs to every vessel in the port, foreign yachts included (Rule 1(b)).

fig.title: Harbour by-laws
lines: Speed limit 5 kn inside the breakwater
Call port control on VHF 12 before entry
No anchoring in the approach channel
Dues payable at the office on arrival

q: The owner was skippering his own yacht when she did the damage below, and the claims exceed the limit for a yacht of her size. Can he limit his liability?
a: No — loss from his own reckless act cannot be limited
o: Yes — any owner may limit, whatever the cause
Yes, but only for the damage to the yachts
No — limitation is only for commercial ships
why: Under the LLMC the right to limit is lost if the loss came from the owner's own act, done recklessly or with intent.

fig.title: The flag state applies the LLMC 1976
lines: Owner at the helm after drinking
Entered harbour at night at 12 kn
Quay and two moored yachts damaged

q: In daylight your deckhand slips off the side deck of your twin-screw 24 m motor yacht at 12 kn. Everyone saw him go and he is in sight astern. Which turn do you make?
a: Anderson turn: hard to starboard, round about 250°, then stop
o: Williamson turn: back onto the reciprocal, search the wake
Scharnow turn: at 240° off, hard over the other way
Hard to port first, to swing the stern away from him
why: Immediate action, casualty in sight, a handy twin-screw yacht: the Anderson turn is quickest; helm to his side swings the props clear.

fig.title: Man overboard
lines: Fell from the starboard side deck
Seen at once, in sight astern

q: At 0420 a guest tells you she saw a crew member go over the side about five minutes ago. No light or beacon went with him. You want to get back into your own wake in the fewest miles. Which turn?
a: Scharnow turn — back into your wake in the least distance
o: Anderson turn — the quickest when you act at once
Williamson turn — the one that covers fewest miles
No turn; press MOB now and the waypoint marks him
why: A late report with the time known: the Scharnow regains your wake in less distance than the Williamson; the Anderson is for immediate action.

fig.title: Late report
lines: Seen going over about 5 min ago
No light or beacon on him

q: You start a Scharnow turn to starboard from the heading below. At what heading do you put the wheel hard over the other way, and on what heading do you steady?
a: Reverse at 010°T; steady on 310°T
o: Reverse at 190°T; steady on 310°T
Reverse at 250°T; steady on 310°T
Reverse at 010°T; steady on 130°T
why: Scharnow: hard over, reverse 240° off the start — 130° + 240° = 010°T — and steady on the reciprocal, 310°T, back in the wake.

q: Your 24 m motor yacht, high-sided with a big flybridge, is coming back to a man in the water in a fresh breeze. How do you make the final approach?
a: Stop upwind of him, beam to the wind, and drift down onto him
o: Come up from downwind, bow to the wind, as in a small yacht
Circle him at speed to flatten the sea around him
Back down on him stern-first so the platform reaches him
why: A high-sided yacht drifts faster than a swimmer: stopped to windward she makes a lee and drifts onto him, props clear of him.
ref: MOB — recovery by a motor yacht

q: Your fixed system has fired by itself in the engine room, and both engines and the generator stopped at the same moment. The mate wants to restart the engines at once. What do you say?
a: No — the shutdown is meant; wait the hold time, then check
o: Yes — override the relay; the shutdown is a fault
Yes — but only the engine on the side with no fire
Yes — engines running will help to clear the gas
why: The system stops engines and fans so they cannot draw the agent out; restart only after the hold time and a check.

q: Under sail in your 23 m ketch, smoke pours from the engine room under the aft cockpit. You have stopped the engine and shut the fuel. How do you put her to the wind while you fight it?
a: Bow to wind and slow, so the smoke blows aft, away from you
o: Run off downwind, so the apparent wind is at its least
Keep reaching fast on this tack to make port sooner
Heave to with the fire on the windward side of you
why: Keep the fire downwind of the crew: with the fire aft, bring her head to wind and slow down so the draught does not fan it.

fig.title: Engine-room fire, aft
lines: Engine room under the aft cockpit
Fire port in the engine-room door

q: On your 15 m catamaran the port engine-compartment alarm sounds and smoke leaks from round its hatch. How do you deal with it?
a: Stop port engine and fuel, use the fire port, steer on the other
o: Stop both engines and lift the hatch to find the fire
Keep the port engine running so its blower clears smoke
Lift the hatch and empty an extinguisher straight in
why: Each hull's engine has its own space: keep the hatch shut, attack through the port, and the other engine keeps you manoeuvring.

fig.title: Catamaran, port hull
lines: Engine under the aft port cabin
Fire port in the compartment lid

q: Your 14 m catamaran hits a floating container 100 M offshore. The port bow fills quickly up to the crash bulkhead and she trims down by the head on that side. What do you do?
a: Stay aboard, slow down, move weight aft to starboard, watch the bulkhead
o: Take to the raft — a holed multihull goes down fast
Pump the bow dry through the hatch in the bulkhead
Move the crew forward to port to settle her evenly
why: The crash bulkhead keeps the rest dry and the other hull floats her: stay aboard, ease the load, take weight off the damaged bow.

fig.title: Damage, port bow
lines: Crash bulkhead holding, a slow weep

q: Two hours after you bounced off a rock ledge, water is seeping round the keel bolts of your 20 m sloop and the floor around them flexes as she pitches. You are 60 M from port, beating in F5. What do you do?
a: Sails down, lifejackets on and raft ready, motor gently to port
o: Keep beating hard to make port before dark
Tighten the keel nuts hard and sail on as before
Bear away and run under full sail to ease her
why: A working keel can drop off and she then capsizes at once: take the sail load off it, prepare to abandon, motor gently.

fig.title: Keel area
lines: Keel floor flexing as she pitches
60 M to port, beating in F5

q: At 2200 the guests' electric surfboard battery, left charging on the aft deck, starts to hiss and smoke. What do you do?
a: Over the side if it can be done safely; if not, flood it with water
o: A CO2 extinguisher — it starves the fire of air
Cover it with a fire blanket and leave it to burn out
One powder extinguisher, then carry it below to cool
why: A lithium pack in thermal runaway feeds itself, so smothering fails: get it overboard or cool it with plenty of water, upwind of the smoke.

fig.title: Aft deck
lines: Deck hose rigged; CO2 and powder near

q: On your 24 m motor yacht the engine room is flooding through a split in the plating behind the engine that nobody can reach, faster than the pumps clear it. What do you do first?
a: Get the engineer out, then shut the watertight door
o: Leave the door open so the mess pumps help as well
Shut the door at once with the engineer still inside
Send more crew in to hunt for the leak
why: A watertight door stops the flood spreading to the next compartment: count everyone out, then close it and keep it shut.

fig.title: Engine room
lines: Split in the plating, out of reach
Watertight door to crew mess open

q: Your yacht is holed 120 M offshore. Her stability notes say she is lost once a further 6 t of water is aboard. How long have you got?
a: About 15 min
o: About 9 min
About 24 min
About 7 min
why: Net inflow 650 − 250 = 400 L/min; 6,000 ÷ 400 = 15 min: send the distress alert and ready the rafts now.

fig.title: Flooding
lines: Stability notes: lost at +6 t (6,000 L)

q: At 1310, 40 min after high water, your 20 m sloop runs onto a sandbank on the falling tide. You look at the tide table. When is your best chance of getting her off?
a: Now, at once — heel, kedge and engine before it falls further
o: Tonight at 0055 — the next high water will lift her off
In about 7 days at neaps, when the streams are weakest
Tomorrow at midday, when the tide is back up to 5.4 m
why: At the top of springs each following high water is lower — 5.2 m tonight against the 5.3 m she needs — so act before the tide drops.

fig.title: Tide table
lines: HWs fall to 3.9 m at neaps in 7 days
She floats with 5.3 m of tide here

q: Your 24 m motor yacht is sinking and the raft is inflated alongside the stern. Your crew are mustered on the boat deck. Where do they board it from?
a: The bathing platform, stepping in dry one at a time
o: The boat deck — jump straight down onto the canopy
The side deck — jump into the sea beside the raft
The boat deck, sliding down the painter into it
why: Board dry from the lowest point: a jump into the raft injures those inside, and a jump into the sea brings cold shock.

fig.title: Heights above the water
lines: Bathing platform: 0.4 m, clear of fire
Raft on its painter at the stern

q: You must abandon your 22 m yacht 130 M offshore with nine aboard. She carries two 8-person rafts. How do you use them?
a: Launch both, share out people and kit, tie them together
o: Launch one and put all nine in it for warmth
Launch both and let them drift apart to widen the search
Launch one and keep the other aboard as a spare
why: One raft would be over its rating; two tied together share the gear, the warmth and the watch, and make one bigger target.

fig.title: Abandoning
lines: Grab bag, EPIRB, SART, handheld VHF

q: Your yacht went down in seconds and three of you are in the water in lifejackets, with no raft. The water is 12°C and the EPIRB is on. How do you wait?
a: Huddle together, chests touching, legs drawn up, and keep still
o: Swim about to keep warm until the helicopter comes
Spread out in a line to be seen from further away
Take turns treading water to keep the blood moving
why: A huddle keeps the heat of chest and groin; swimming or treading water pumps cold water past the skin and cools you faster.

fig.title: In the water
lines: Three crew, lifejackets on, no raft
EPIRB floating, tied to one of you

q: You went into the water two minutes ago and your breathing has just settled. The raft is held on its painter to floating wreckage 50 m away. What do you do?
a: Swim for it now, while your arms still work
o: Hold still in the HELP position and wait
Wait some more minutes for the cold shock to pass
Take off the lifejacket so you can swim faster
why: 1-10-1: a minute of cold shock, about ten of useful movement, an hour before hypothermia: use those ten minutes to save yourself now.

fig.title: In the water
lines: In for 2 min; gasping has eased
Raft on its painter to wreckage, 50 m

q: You have gone over the side alone, in a lifejacket, and the yacht is turning back for you — it may take 20 minutes. How do you hold yourself while you wait?
a: Knees drawn up, arms crossed over the chest, still: the HELP
o: Swimming slowly after the yacht to close the gap
Lying flat on your back, arms and legs spread out
Upright and treading water to keep your head higher
why: The HELP posture guards the armpits, chest and groin, where most heat is lost; every movement spends heat and strength.

q: The helicopter pilot asks you to hold a steady speed with the wind 30° on your port bow while he winches. What heading do you steer?
why: Port bow means the wind comes from 30° to port of the heading: 040° + 30° = 070°T; 010°T would put it on the starboard bow.

fig.title: Winching
lines: Pilot: wind 30° on the port bow
Steady speed 8 kn, hold the heading

q: Midway across, a crew member who takes insulin turns pale, sweaty, shaky and muddled before lunch. He can still swallow. What do you do first?
a: Sugar now — a sweet drink or glucose — then food and advice
o: His insulin dose now, to bring his sugar back down
Nothing by mouth; lay him down and let him sleep
Wait an hour to see whether it passes by itself
why: Low blood sugar: sugar by mouth while he can swallow brings him round fast; more insulin would make it far worse.

fig.title: Crew member
lines: Missed breakfast, seasick in the night

q: Dismasted and cut free 120 M from the nearest port, you check the fuel. Keeping the reserve, can you motor all the way in?
a: No — about 96 M; rig a jury sail as well
o: Yes — exactly 120 M, just enough to arrive
Yes — about 144 M, with some to spare
No — about 54 M; call for a tow at once
why: Usable 90 × 0.8 = 72 L; 72 ÷ 4.5 = 16 h; 16 h × 6 kn = 96 M — short of 120 M, so a jury rig must make up the rest.

q: On your 20 m yacht the wheel turns but the rudder no longer answers: the helm pump has failed. You ship the emergency tiller on the stock, but it will hardly move. What have you missed?
a: Opening the bypass valve on the ram so the oil can pass
o: Bleeding the air out of the helm pump first
Topping up the oil in the helm pump reservoir
Lashing the wheel amidships to hold the rudder
why: Oil trapped in the ram locks the rudder; the bypass (crossover) valve lets it flow from side to side so the tiller can work.

fig.title: Steering
lines: Hydraulic ram on the rudder quadrant
Helm pump failed, no leak found
Emergency tiller fitted on the stock

q: At 0100 in F6 a guest coming on watch refuses to clip on, saying he has sailed for thirty years. You are the skipper. What do you do?
a: Insist: he clips on or he stays below — your order stands
o: Let him decide — he is an adult and an experienced sailor
Ask the owner aboard to settle it in the morning
Note his refusal in the log and let him go up
why: The skipper answers for the safety of everyone aboard, and his safety orders bind guests and crew alike.

q: Your yacht is sinking 120 M offshore. A ship shows on AIS 8 M away, and you have a VHF DSC set and a satellite phone with the MRCC's number. What do you do first?
a: VHF DSC alert and MAYDAY on 16, then phone the MRCC
o: Phone the MRCC first: it can task the ship itself
Call the ship on 16 by name, without a MAYDAY
DSC individual call to the ship, then talk on 72
why: A DSC alert and a MAYDAY reach every ship in range at once; a phone call reaches only the MRCC, and the ship 8 M off hears nothing.

fig.title: Your kit
lines: Satellite phone, MRCC number in it
Ship on AIS 8 M away, closing
No coast station in VHF range

q: At 1300 you are calling a distant coast station on your HF set, and on 4 MHz it is faint and broken. What do you try next?
a: A higher band, such as 8 or 12 MHz
o: A lower band, such as 2 MHz on MF
4 MHz again at full power until it clears
VHF channel 16, which carries further by day
why: By day the sky wave carries the higher HF bands further: over a long distance in daylight move up a band, at night move down.

q: At 0300 you must send an HF DSC urgency call to the coast station below for medical advice. Following its guide, on which frequency do you call?
a: 6312 kHz
why: 0300 is night: 650 M falls in the 6 MHz band (500–1,000 M), so 6312 kHz; the day table would give 8 MHz.

fig.title: Coast station guide (HF DSC)
lines: Day: 4 MHz to 300 M, 8 to 800 M, 12 beyond
Night: 4 MHz to 500 M, 6 to 1,000 M, 8 beyond
You are 650 M from the station

q: In the raft, your grab bag holds an AIS-SART, not a radar SART. A ship is closing at night. Where will her watchkeeper see you?
a: As a SART target with your position on her AIS display
o: As a line of 12 dots on her radar screen
Only on the MRCC's screen, through the satellites
Nowhere until she comes within about a mile
why: An AIS-SART sends its GPS position as an AIS message: it shows on AIS displays and plotters, not on radar like a radar SART.

fig.title: Grab bag
lines: AIS-SART switched on, up on its pole

q: You are standing by a yacht in distress 3 M away. On 16 two other yachts keep chatting over her calls, and no coast station is in range. What may you say?
a: SEELONCE DISTRESS, then your yacht's name
o: SEELONCE MAYDAY, then your yacht's name
SEELONCE FEENEE, then your yacht's name
PRUDONCE, then your yacht's name
why: Only the casualty or the station controlling the traffic says SEELONCE MAYDAY; another station near her imposes silence with SEELONCE DISTRESS.

fig.title: Channel 16
lines: MAYDAY from a yacht 3 M off, ongoing
You are not controlling the traffic

q: Alongside after the passage, you notice the EPIRB in its bracket flashing: it has been transmitting for an hour. Nothing is wrong. What do you do?
a: Switch it off and tell the nearest MRCC it was a false alert
o: Switch it off and say nothing — no harm was done
Leave it on until the MRCC calls you about it
Take the battery out so it cannot happen again
why: A 406 MHz alert has started a search somewhere; switch off and tell the MRCC at once so that they can stand it down.

q: At 0400, 140 M offshore, your MF DSC set receives a distress alert from a vessel 380 M away. A minute later a coast station acknowledges it by DSC. What do you do?
a: Listen on 2182 kHz and log it; help only if asked
o: Send a DSC relay to all ships to spread the word
Acknowledge it by DSC so she knows she was heard
Turn and head for her at your best speed now
why: Once a coast station has acknowledged, the alert is in hand: watch the voice frequency, log it, and stand by to help if asked.

q: You are 2 h into a 40 M run towards a liferaft when the MRCC calls you with the message below. What do you do?
a: Resume your passage and log the release with the time
o: Carry on to the raft — only her crew can release you
Carry on until you see the ship take them aboard
Resume your passage; there is nothing to log
why: SOLAS V/33: once told that other ships have been requisitioned and are complying, you are released; record it in the log.

fig.title: MRCC on channel 16
lines: Ship 'Nordic Star' 4 M from the raft
She has been tasked and is proceeding
You are released from the search

q: The MRCC asks ships near a sinking fishing boat 70 M away to go to her. By your figures you can reach her, but then no port with the fuel left. What does SOLAS require of you?
a: Tell the MRCC you cannot go, and log the reason
o: Go anyway — the duty to assist comes before your safety
Say nothing on the radio; others will answer the call
Log the call, but there is no need to answer the MRCC
why: V/33.1: a master who is unable to assist must enter the reason in the log and inform the SAR service — never just stay silent.

fig.title: Your position
lines: Nearest fuel after her: 110 M on

q: At 0200, 130 M offshore, the wind rises to a steady force 10. The last forecast, two hours ago, gave force 6 to 7 with no gale warning. What does SOLAS V/31 ask of you?
a: Report it to the coast station and to ships nearby
o: Nothing — reports are for ice and derelicts only
Report it only if the yacht is damaged by it
Record it in your log; report it at your next port
why: V/31: a master who meets winds of force 10 or more with no storm warning received must pass it on to ships near and the coast.

q: At night you collide with a sailing yacht. Nobody is hurt and your own damage is above the waterline. Before you go on, what must you do for her?
a: Stand by until she needs no help, and give your yacht's details
o: Nothing more — nobody was hurt in the collision
Exchange insurers' names, then continue at once
Stand by only if she was the stand-on vessel
why: After a collision the master must help the other vessel and her people, so far as he safely can, and give his ship's name and port of registry.

fig.title: After the collision
lines: Crew of four, no injuries reported
Your bow damaged above the waterline

q: You are moving your yacht from one flag to another. Before the new registry will enter her, what does it want from the old one?
a: A deletion certificate: closed, with no mortgage left on it
o: A copy of her current certificate of registry
Nothing — she may stay on both registers for a year
A letter from the builder confirming her hull number
why: A ship may fly one flag only: the new register needs proof the old registration is closed and no mortgage is still recorded on it.

fig.title: Change of flag
lines: Registered on flag A, mortgage paid off
Flag B's form asks for an old-register paper

q: The owner has gone bankrupt and the yacht is sold for less than her debts. In what order are the three lenders paid from the sale?
a: B, then A, then C
o: C, then A, then B
A, then B, then C
B, then C, then A
why: Registered mortgages rank by date of entry, not of signing — B (12 Mar) before A (20 Mar) — and the unregistered C comes last.

fig.title: Mortgages on the register
lines: Rule: by date entered; unregistered last

q: You bought this registered yacht 40 days ago and have sent nothing to the registry yet. You plan to sail for a foreign port tomorrow. Where do you stand?
a: She is unregistered — apply and get papers before you sail
o: Fine — the seller's certificate covers her until renewal
Fine — the bill of sale aboard proves her nationality
Fine — the registry is needed only for a new name
why: Past the 30 days her registration has lapsed: without a valid certificate she has no proven nationality abroad.

fig.title: Flag's registry rules
lines: On a sale, registration lapses in 30 days
unless the buyer applies with the bill of sale
Certificate aboard: in the seller's name
Bought 40 days ago, no application yet

q: Your employer has taken this yacht on a bareboat charter for the summer and you are her skipper. The owner, aboard as a guest for a weekend, orders you to change the passage plan. Whose instructions do you follow?
a: The charterer's — the owner gave up control for the charter
o: The owner's — the yacht is his, charter or not
Whoever is aboard — the owner, since he is here
The insurer's — the policy names the owner
why: Under a bareboat charter the charterer takes possession and control and engages the skipper; the owner aboard is only a guest.

fig.title: Charter
lines: Owner aboard as a guest this weekend
He wants to go to a different island

q: Your flag applies the MLC rest rules to your paid deckhands. Looking at their last 24 hours below, who has broken them?
a: Ben and Carl — no 6 h spell
o: Nobody — all three had 10 h
Ben only — he has three spells
All three — rest must be unbroken
why: All had 10 h, but Ben's comes in three spells and neither of Carl's two reaches 6 h; only Anna's 6 + 4 meets the rule.

fig.title: Deckhands' rest, last 24 h
lines: MLC: 10 h rest/24 h, ≤2 spells, one ≥6 h

q: Your paid deckhand breaks his wrist in a foreign port and is signed off to fly home. Under your flag's rules below, who pays for his flight?
a: The owner, as his employer
o: The deckhand himself
You, as the skipper who signed him on
The port's health authority
why: MLC: a seafarer signed off sick or injured in service is repatriated at the employer's cost — here the owner.

fig.title: Flag: paid crew (MLC 2006)
lines: Written agreement for every paid crew
if sick or injured in service

q: Under Lloyd's Open Form a salvor towed your disabled yacht off a lee shore. As saved she is worth €380,000, and he claims €420,000 for a hard job. What can the award be?
a: Some part of the €380,000 — never more than that
o: The full €420,000 — he decides what the job was worth
€380,000, plus his costs over and above it
A fixed tariff by length, whatever he claims
why: Salvage Convention art. 13: the award is fixed on the listed factors but may not exceed the value of the property salved.

fig.title: Salvage claim
lines: Danger high, skill and effort great

q: In a storm a fishing boat took your crew off your sinking yacht. Next day a tug found her still afloat and saved her under LOF. The fishermen ask whether they are owed anything. What is the answer?
a: A fair share of the tug's award, as they saved the lives
o: Nothing — saving lives earns no payment at all
Their own award, paid by your crew for saving them
The whole award — they were on the scene first
why: Art. 16: the people saved owe nothing, but a life salvor in the same casualty shares fairly in the award for saving the yacht.

fig.title: Two rescues
lines: Day 1: fishing boat saves the crew
Day 2: tug salves the yacht under LOF

q: Your disabled yacht is being towed in under LOF and the salvage master asks you to keep a bilge pump running and a lookout aft. What is your duty?
a: Co-operate fully and do what he reasonably asks
o: None — the salvor now answers for everything
Refuse — as skipper you take orders from nobody
Only what your insurer has approved in writing
why: Salvage Convention art. 8: the owner and master must co-operate fully with the salvor and take the yacht back once she is safe.

fig.title: Under LOF
lines: Asks: bilge pump on, lookout aft
You are still aboard with 3 crew

q: You agreed a fixed price for a tug to tow your yacht, engine dead, 40 M to port. Halfway a gale gets up, she starts to flood, and the tug's crew come aboard and pump for six hours to save her. What can the tug claim?
a: Salvage for the extra work, beyond the towage price
o: Only the €4,000 — the price was fixed in advance
Nothing — salvage needs LOF signed at the time
Double the price, as the job was harder than agreed
why: Art. 17: work under a contract earns salvage only when it goes beyond the contract's due performance — as when a new danger arises.

fig.title: The tow
lines: Tug's crew pump for 6 h and save her
No danger when the tow was agreed

q: Becalmed and in no danger, you clearly refuse a fishing boat's offer of a tow, and say so on 16. She makes fast to your bow anyway, tows you in and claims salvage. What is she owed?
a: Nothing — you refused her clearly and with good reason
o: A salvage reward, which any towed vessel owes
Her fuel only, since she did save you time
A reward, but halved as you did not ask for it
why: No danger, no salvage; and art. 19 gives nothing for services forced on you against an express and reasonable refusal.

fig.title: On channel 16, 1420
lines: You: no danger, no tow wanted, thanks

q: While you take on fuel alongside, the nozzle sticks open and about 20 L of diesel goes over the side into the harbour. Once the flow is stopped, what do you do?
a: Report it to the harbour office and help contain it
o: Spray detergent on it so it breaks up quickly
Say nothing — 20 L will be gone within the hour
Hose it away from the pontoon with deck water
why: An oil spill must be reported to the port or coastal authority at once; detergent only sinks it and makes the harm worse.

fig.title: Fuel berth
lines: About 20 L of diesel in the water
Absorbent boom at the fuel kiosk

q: At 1530, 80 M offshore, you pass through a long, fresh oil slick with a tanker on AIS steaming away from its end. What do you do?
a: Report it to the coast station: position, extent, ship
o: Nothing — reporting pollution is the tanker's own duty
Call the tanker on 16 and tell her to stop it
Photograph it and post it online for the authorities
why: Coastal states rely on sightings: give the coast station or MRCC the slick's position and size and the ship suspected.

fig.title: Slick
lines: Slick 2 M long, fresh and dark
Tanker on AIS at its end, 3 M off
Your position, time and her name noted

q: Your yacht's particulars are below. What does MARPOL Annex V require of her about garbage?
a: Placards on the discharge rules, displayed aboard
o: A garbage record book with every disposal in it
A garbage management plan and a record book
Nothing — Annex V does not apply to yachts
why: Annex V: every ship of 12 m or more shows the placards; the plan starts at 100 GT or 15 persons, the record book at 400 GT.

q: Your 15.4 m catamaran, six aboard, stays three nights in this harbour. What do you pay?

fig.title: Harbour dues
lines: LOA rounded up to the next whole metre
Tourist tax €1.50 per person per night

q: You arrive at a bay inside a marine reserve, and the pilot book prints the notice below. Where do you anchor your 22 m yacht?
a: You don't: you pick up one of the reserve's buoys
o: On the seagrass, which holds well, with plenty of chain
In sand beside the seagrass, the chain lying over it
Anywhere — the rule is for local boats only
why: Local rules bind visiting yachts too: over 20 m this reserve wants you on a buoy, and its posidonia is protected.

fig.title: Marine reserve notice
lines: Yachts over 20 m: mooring buoys only
